Etymology: 15. Bng. ċɔ̀̄ n.f. ‘puddle, pool, plash’ and perhaps with an -r suffix ċɔ̀̄r n.f. ‘a small pond’, Deog. ċɔ̄ ‘waterplace for cattle’ and cɔ̄r ‘a hollow wooden log with a lid to keep water cool in summer (a traditional device)’, and Jaun. cɔ̄l ‘pond’ — Paš. čā ‘well, pool’, Dara. čʌkʌṛ ‘pond’, Wg. ċor ‘pond, pool’ (Z.), Ash. čā ‘a well’ ← Pers. cāh ‘water well’ probably partly via similar forms in many Eastern Iranian languages (like e.g. Shgh. čā ‘a well’). But some of the forms, e.g. Bng. ċɔ̀̄, may derive or are influenced by OIA cyota- ‘oozing, sprinkling’ (4947) and note here Bng. ċɔ̄ṇɔ v.i. ‘to seep or ooze away, soak’ which is < OIA cyótati ‘trickles, oozes’ (4948). Notes: (a) Cf. also Brah. čurri ‘streamlet’, Brah., Bal., Psht. čur ‘small hill-stream’ (Brah. also jhur borrowed ← OIA *jhāra- [5373] ‘flowing’) which compare with OIA curī- ‘small well or reservoir near a well’ (4873); regarding Brah. čurro ‘urine’ see (p. 591). (b) Cf. also with similar meanings Bal. čāt, čʰāθ ‘well, spring’ (Korn [2005: 227]) and Wkh. cal ‘humid, viscous’, and Kho. cat ‘pool, lake’ the last of which Mor- genstierne regards as a borrowing from a Proto-Wakhi form (1926: 76). However, later-on (1936: 660) he quotes Kho. čat, čhat and Kal. c̣hʌt both ‘lake’ (but Trail and Cooper have čhat) and says that borrowing from an Iranian language is “very doubtful.” (c) In case of Brah. čurro ‘urine’, very similar Bur. (child language) ćúro ‘urine’ and, also with meaning ‘urine’, Bng. ċɔra n.m. ‘water; cow’s urine’ and Garh. careṇḍu ‘a pond caused by cattle’s urine’ (with second component -eṇḍu < *ḍhaṇḍha- ‘mud, pool’ [5578]) and cirāṇ, carāṇ ‘stink of urine’ (with -āṇ < OIA ghrāṇá- ‘smell’) there might be contamination of reflexes of OIA *kṣarā- ‘water’ (3662) and an Austro-Asiatic lemma: cf. Monic Nyah Kur crúh ‘urinate’ and per- haps Semelai chɒ̃r ‘be urinated on’ (also ʄrʄɒr ‘urinate’) and Pacoh sṵr ‘sound of poured water, e.g. urinating into water’. Sant. caraʔc curuʔc ‘the sound of milk falling into the pail in small quantity’ and similar forms expressing sounds of dripping are probably closer to ideophones discussed pp. 591 and 257. (d) Old Him. carā, calā, caḷā ‘watercourse, channel’ (Chhabra [1957: 183]) might here not be cognate but just a reflex of OIA CAR ‘move’.
